title.en: The Boy Who Set a Snare for the Sun

region.en: Earth's eastern edge where the sun rises (symbolic pin at dawn horizon)
region.zh: 太陽升起的大地東緣（象徵性定位於黎明的地平線）

texts.period: From the Odjibwa (Schoolcraft 1856); a myth of the origin of the dormouse

source.work: H. R. Schoolcraft, The Myth of Hiawatha, and Other Oral Legends (1856), 'The Sun-Catcher'

summary.en: When the animals reigned, a pygmy brother and sister are the last humans. The boy shoots snow birds for a coat, naps on a melted knoll, and wakes to find the hot sun has singed his bird-skin coat binding him fast; he fasts ten days on each side and then bids his sister make him a snare for the sun. Deer sinew will not do, her hair will not do - at last she twists a cord from her own body, which he draws through his lips, turning it into red metal. He snares the sun at the earth's rim so it does not rise; the animal council sends the dormouse - then the largest animal in the world, mountain-like - whose smoking back is burned to heaps of ashes as it cuts the cord; freed, the sun rises, and the dormouse has remained tiny ever since: men call it Kug-e-been-gwa-kwa, the blind woman.
summary.zh: 群獸統治大地時，一對侏儒姊弟是僅存的人類。弟弟射雪鳥製衣，在雪融的高丘小憩，醒來發現烈日把他的鳥皮衣烤得緊束其身；他兩側各齋戒十日，命姊姊為太陽設網。鹿筋不中用，頭髮不中用——最後她自身抽絲搓繩，弟弟以唇拉引，繩遂化為紅銅。他在大地邊緣縛住太陽，日遂不升；獸會遣當時世上最大的動物——鼯鼠——前去割繩，其背被烈日烤成灰燼之丘；太陽得釋而升，鼯鼠從此變得極小，人稱之為「盲婦」。

sensitivity.note: Odjibwa sun-snare myth (Schoolcraft 1856); public domain. Anchor record of the world-wide 'sun captured' cluster (cf. polynesian Maui).

passages.text: At the time when the animals reigned in the earth, they had killed all but a girl, and her little brother, and these two were living in fear and seclusion. The boy was a perfect pigmy, and never grew beyond the stature of a small infant, but the girl increased with her years, so that the labor of providing food and lodging devolved wholly on her. She made him a bow and arrows, and said to him one day, 'I will leave you behind where I have been chopping - you must hide yourself, and you will soon see the Gitshee-gitshee-gaun-ia-see-ug, or snow birds... Shoot one of them and bring it home.' He obeyed her, and at nightfall came in exultingly and threw down one of the birds which he had killed: 'My sister, I wish you to skin it and stretch the skin, and when I have killed more, I will have a coat made out of them.'
passages.note: Condensed from Schoolcraft 1856, pp. 239-240; not verbatim.

passages.text: After walking a long time and meeting nothing, he became tired, and lay down on a knoll, where the sun had melted the snow. He fell fast asleep; and while sleeping, the sun beat so hot upon him that it singed and drew up his bird-skin coat, so that when he awoke and stretched himself, he felt bound in it, as it were. He flew into a passion, and upbraided the sun, and vowed vengeance against it. 'Do not think you are too high,' said he, 'I shall revenge myself.' He lay down as one that fasts, and did not stir for ten days, though she tried all she could to arouse him; at the end of ten days he turned over, and then lay ten days on the other side. When he got up, he told his sister to make him a snare, for he meant to catch the sun.
passages.note: Condensed from Schoolcraft 1856, pp. 240-241; not verbatim.

passages.text: She said she had nothing; but finally recollected a little piece of dried deer's sinew, which she soon made into a string suitable for a noose; but the moment she showed it to him, he told her it would not do. She said she had nothing - nothing at all; at last she thought of her hair, and pulling some of it out of her head made a string; but he instantly said it would not answer. She went out of the lodge, and said to herself, while she was all alone, 'Now obewy indapin' - from my body I will take something. This she did, and twisting it into a tiny cord, she handed it to her brother. The moment he saw this curious braid he was delighted: 'It will do,' he said, and immediately put it to his mouth and began pulling it through his lips; and as fast as he drew it he changed it into a red metal cord, which he wound around his body and shoulders. He then prepared himself, and set out a little after midnight, that he might catch the sun before it rose: he fixed his snare on a spot just where the sun would strike the land, as it rose above the earth's disk; and sure enough, he caught the sun, so that it was held fast in the cord, and did not rise.
passages.note: Condensed from Schoolcraft 1856, p. 241; not verbatim.

passages.text: The animals who ruled the earth were immediately put into a great commotion. They had no light. They called a council to debate upon the matter, and to appoint some one to go and cut the cord - for this was a very hazardous enterprise, as the rays of the sun would burn whoever came so near to them. At last the dormouse undertook it - for at this time the dormouse was the largest animal in the world: when it stood up it looked like a mountain. When it got to the place where the sun was snared, its back began to smoke and burn with the intensity of the heat, and the top of its carcass was reduced to enormous heaps of ashes. It succeeded, however, in cutting the cord with its teeth, and freeing the sun, but it was reduced to a very small size, and has remained so ever since. Men call it the Kug-e-been-gwa-kwa - the blind woman.
passages.note: Condensed from Schoolcraft 1856, pp. 241-242; not verbatim.

title.en: Eroneniera: An Indian Visit to the Great Spirit (Told by Pontiac, 1763)
title.zh: 伊羅尼埃拉：拜見生命之主（龐蒂亞克1763年所述）

region.en: Mountain of marvellous whiteness (symbolic pin in the upper Great Lakes)
region.zh: 奇白如雪的高山（象徵性定位於上大湖區）

texts.period: Told by Pontiac to the assembled Indians in 1763, to enlist them against the English transfer of the country (recorded by Schoolcraft, 1856)

source.work: H. R. Schoolcraft, The Myth of Hiawatha, and Other Oral Legends (1856), 'Eroneniera; or, an Indian visit to the Great Spirit'

summary.en: An Indian resolved to see the Master of Life follows three paths for as many days, past fires issuing from the ground, until a mountain of marvellous whiteness rises before him, where a dazzling woman directs him to strip, wash in the river, and climb with left hand and foot only. Admitted through the gate by a man dressed all in white, he is seated on a gold-bordered hat by the Master of Life, who proclaims the moral laws - no drunkenness, one wife, no medicine song ('it is to the Manito that you speak') - commands the Indians to drive off the invaders, and gives him a written prayer to teach to all the Indians, morning and evening.
summary.zh: 一位印第安人立志面見生命之主，循三條路各行一日，經過地底噴火之處，終於望見一座奇白的高山；山上光豔的女子命他卸除衣裝、在河中淨身，僅以左手左足攀頂。白袍男子啟門引入，生命之主命他坐在鑲金的帽子上，宣布道德律令——戒酗酒、一夫一妻、禁唱藥歌（「你們是在對惡靈說話」）——並命印第安人驅逐入侵者，賜他一篇書寫的祈禱文，命他朝夕教授給所有印第安人。

sensitivity.note: Schoolcraft 1856; public domain. Schoolcraft notes Pontiac told this to the assembled Indians in 1763 to enlist resistance to the English - a political theophany of record.

passages.text: He walked a long time without being discouraged, having always a firm conviction that he should attain his aim. On the evening of the eighth day, at sunset, he stopped as usual on the bank of a brook, at the entrance of a little prairie, and perceived at the other end three very wide and well-beaten paths; the darker it grew, the more distinct were those paths, which surprised, nay, even frightened him. He remembered his dream, and thought that his only aim in undertaking his journey was to see the Master of Life. He left his encampment and fire, and took the widest of the paths; he followed it until the middle of the day, when he suddenly perceived a large fire coming from under ground, and, as it appeared to increase as he drew nearer, he was so overcome with fear that he turned back and took the widest of the other two paths - in which, after the same space of time, he perceived a similar spectacle, and was obliged to take the third path.
passages.note: Condensed from Schoolcraft 1856, pp. 252-253; not verbatim.

passages.text: All at once, a mountain of a marvellous whiteness burst upon his sight. At the foot he saw no signs of a road; looking on all sides he perceived a female seated upon the mountain, her beauty dazzling, and the whiteness of her garments surpassing that of snow. The woman said to him in his own language, 'You appear surprised to find no longer a path to reach your wishes... The way which leads to his abode is upon this mountain. To ascend it, you must undress yourself completely, and leave all your accoutrements and clothing at the foot... You will then go and wash yourself in the river which I am now showing you, and afterward ascend the mountain.' He asked how he was to accomplish it; she replied that if he really wished to see the Master of Life, he must, in mounting, only use his left hand and foot. When at the top he found himself alone, without a guide; three unknown villages were in sight, constructed on a different plan from his own, much handsomer and more regular.
passages.note: Condensed from Schoolcraft 1856, pp. 253-254; not verbatim.

passages.text: When about half way from the top of the mountain, he recollected that he was naked, and was afraid to proceed; but a voice told him to advance, and have no apprehensions. He proceeded to a place which appeared to be the gate of the village; the gate opened, and the Indian saw coming towards him a handsome man dressed all in white, who took him by the hand and said he was going to satisfy his wishes by leading him to the presence of the Master of Life. They arrived at a place of unequalled beauty. The Indian there saw the Master of Life, who took him by the hand and gave him for a seat a hat bordered with gold.
passages.note: Condensed from Schoolcraft 1856, pp. 254-255; not verbatim.

passages.text: God said to him, 'I am the Master of Life, whom thou wishest to see... I am the Maker of Heaven and earth, the trees, lakes, rivers, men, and all that thou seest or hast seen on the earth or in the heavens; and because I love you, you must do my will... I hate you to drink as you do, until you lose your reason; I wish you not to fight one another; you take two wives, or run after other people's wives; you do wrong... When you go to war, you juggle, you sing the medicine song, thinking you speak to me; you deceive yourselves; it is to the Manito that you speak; he is a wicked spirit who induces you to evil. The land on which you are, I have made for you, not for others: wherefore do you suffer the whites to dwell upon your lands?... Drive them away; wage war against them. I love them not. They know me not... Here is a written prayer which I give thee; learn it by heart, and teach it to all the Indians and children... It must be repeated morning and evening.' His conductor then came, and leading him to the foot of the mountain, told him to take his garments and return to his village; having entered the village, he went immediately to the chief's wigwam and delivered to him the prayer and laws intrusted to his care by the Master of Life.
passages.note: Condensed from Schoolcraft 1856, pp. 255-257; not verbatim.

title.en: The Six Hawks; or, Broken Wing: An Allegory of Fraternal Affection
title.zh: 六鷹：折翼——手足之情之喻

region.en: Northern woods where the falcons winter in a hollow tree
region.zh: 北地樹洞中越冬的鷹巢

texts.period: An allegory of fraternal affection collected by Schoolcraft (1856)

source.work: H. R. Schoolcraft, The Myth of Hiawatha, and Other Oral Legends (1856), 'The Six Hawks'

summary.en: Both parent falcons are shot in one day, leaving six young birds. The eldest, Meeji-geeg-wona the Gray Eagle, feeds the brood until he breaks a wing pouncing on a swan; the brothers refuse the southern journey: 'If the climate kills you, it shall kill us.' They winter together in a hollow tree, two going south to lighten the store, until the Gray Eagle recovers and instructs them in hunting. The foolish Pigeon Hawk is robbed of every kill by a great white owl, which the Gray Eagle seizes; they counsel mercy - 'this will be a lesson to him not to tyrannize over any one who is weaker than himself' - and release the owl, which teaches what herbs will cure its wounds. The two southern nestmates return and all fly off to mate: 'these six birds only represent one of our impoverished northern families of children, who had been deprived of both their parents and the aid of their elder brother nearly at the same time.'
summary.zh: 雙親鷹一日之間雙雙被射殺，留下六隻幼鷹。長兄「灰鷹」米吉格格沃納哺育弟妹，直到撲殺天鵝時折損一翼；眾弟妹拒絕南飛：「若寒氣殺你，便連我們一起殺。」眾鷹同住樹洞過冬，兩隻南飛以省存糧；灰鷹傷癒後授以獵術。愚笨的鴿鷹屢被大白鴞劫掠獵物，灰鷹遂擒之；眾鷹勸以寬恕——「讓牠從此不敢欺凌弱小」——放鴞而去，並教牠治傷的草藥。南歸的二鷹返巢團聚，各擇佳偶飛入林中：「這六隻鳥，代表的正是我們北方那些同時失去雙親與長兄照拂的貧苦家庭。」

passages.text: There were six young falcons living in a nest, all but one of whom were still unable to fly, when it so happened that both the parent birds were shot by the hunters in one day. The young brood waited with impatience for their return; but night came, and they were left without parents and without food. Meeji-geeg-wona, or the Gray Eagle, the eldest, and the only one whose feathers had become stout enough to enable him to leave the nest, assumed the duty of stilling their cries and providing them with food, in which he was very successful. But, after a short time had passed, he, by an unlucky mischance, got one of his wings broken in pouncing upon a swan.
passages.note: Verbatim from Schoolcraft 1856, p. 258; not verbatim (OCR modernized).

passages.text: 'Brothers,' he said, 'an accident has befallen me, but let not this prevent your going to a warmer climate. Winter is rapidly approaching, and you cannot remain here. It is better that I alone should die than for you all to suffer miserably on my account.' 'No! no!' they replied, with one voice, 'we will not forsake you; we will share your sufferings; we will abandon our journey, and take care of you, as you did of us... If the climate kills you, it shall kill us... Whether you live or die, we will live or die with you.' They sought out a hollow tree to winter in, and contrived to carry their wounded nestmate there; and, before the rigors of winter set in, they had stored up food enough to carry them through its severities. To make it last the better, two of the number went off south, leaving the other three to watch over, feed, and protect the wounded bird.
passages.note: Verbatim from Schoolcraft 1856, pp. 258-259; not verbatim (OCR modernized).

passages.text: Meeji-geeg-wona in due time recovered from his wound, and he repaid their kindness by giving them such advice and instruction in the art of hunting as his experience had qualified him to impart. The youngest, Peepi-geewi-zains, the Pigeon Hawk, always came back without anything: 'It is not my smallness or weakness of body... I kill ducks and other birds every time I go out; but, just as I get to the woods, a large Ko-ko-ko-ho robs me of my prey.' 'Well! don't despair, brother,' said Meeji-geeg-wona. 'I now feel my strength perfectly recovered, and I will go out with you to-morrow.' They went forth in company, and when the white owl claimed the pigeon hawk's prize, the Gray Eagle came up, and, fixing his talons in both sides of the owl, flew home with him.
passages.note: Verbatim from Schoolcraft 1856, pp. 259-260; not verbatim (OCR modernized).

passages.text: The little pigeon hawk flew in the owl's face and vented his passion in abundance of reproachful terms. 'Softly,' said the Gray Eagle; 'do not be in such a passion, or exhibit so revengeful a disposition; for this will be a lesson to him not to tyrannize over any one who is weaker than himself for the future.' So, after giving him good advice, and telling him what kind of herbs would cure his wounds, they let the owl go. While this act was taking place, two visitors appeared at the hollow tree - the two nestmates who had just returned from the south; they were thus all happily reunited, and each one soon chose a mate and flew off to the woods. Spring had now revisited the north... 'But it is in vain,' said the old man who related this story, 'that spring returns, if we are not thankful to the Master of Life who has preserved us through the winter... These six birds only represent one of our impoverished northern families of children, who had been deprived of both their parents and the aid of their elder brother nearly at the same time.'
passages.note: Verbatim from Schoolcraft 1856, pp. 260-261; not verbatim (OCR modernized).

region.en: Hunter's lodge and smoking pouch of the Odjibwa woods
region.zh: 奧吉布瓦林中的獵屋與菸草袋

source.work: H. R. Schoolcraft, The Myth of Hiawatha, and Other Oral Legends (1856), 'Weeng, the spirit of sleep'

summary.en: Sleep is personified by the Odjibwas under the name of Weeng, executed by gnome-like beings each armed with a tiny war-club, with which they nimbly climb up the forehead and knock the drowsy person on the head until the eyelids close. They hide in the smoking pouch of the hunter, ready to fly out when he sits down to light his pipe - and the game passes. Iagoo's tale: losing his dogs in a thicket, he found them asleep near Weeng's residence, and saw the Spirit of Sleep himself on a tree branch, a giant insect-like monetos with many wings making a low deep murmuring sound like distant falling water - 'but Iagoo himself, being a very great liar and braggart, but little credit was given to his narration.' Weeng is also the author of dulness: if an orator fails, he is struck by Weeng.
summary.zh: 奧吉布瓦人以「溫格」之名化身睡眠；其職司由一群手持小戰棒的精怪執行——牠們靈巧地爬上額頭，敲擊昏昏欲睡者的頭，直至眼瞼闔上。牠們藏在獵人的菸草袋中，待其坐下點菸時飛出施術——獵物便趁機逸去。亞古的故事：他在密林中丟了獵犬，尋見牠們睡在溫格居所附近；抬頭看見睡眠之靈坐在樹枝上——狀如多翼的巨蟲，發出如遠處流水般的低沉嗡鳴——「但亞古是出了名的吹牛大王，人們自然不大相信。」溫格還是沉悶之源：演說失敗，便說是被溫格擊中了。

passages.text: Sleep is personified by the Odjibwas under the name of Weeng. The power of the Indian Morpheus is executed by a peculiar class of gnome-like beings, called Weengs. These subordinate creations, although invisible to the human eye, are each armed with a tiny war-club, or puggamaugun, with which they nimbly climb up the forehead, and knock the drowsy person on the head; on which sleepiness is immediately produced. If the first blow is insufficient, another is given, until the eyelids close, and a sound sleep is produced. It is the constant duty of these little agents to put every one to sleep whom they encounter - men, women, and children. And they are found secreted around the bed, or on small protuberances of the bark of the Indian lodges.
passages.note: Verbatim from Schoolcraft 1856, p. 262; not verbatim (OCR modernized).

passages.text: They hide themselves in the Gushkeepitaugun, or smoking pouch of the hunter, and when he sits down to light his pipe in the woods, are ready to fly out and exert their sleep-compelling power. If they succeed, the game is suffered to pass, and the hunter obliged to return to his lodge without a reward. In general, however, they are represented to possess friendly dispositions, seeking constantly to restore vigor and elasticity to the exhausted body. But being without judgment, their power is sometimes exerted at the hazard of reputation, or even life... If an orator fails, he is said to be struck by Weeng. If a warrior lingers, he has ventured too near the sleepy god. If children begin to nod or yawn, the Indian mother looks up smilingly, and says, 'They have been struck by Weeng,' and puts them to bed.
passages.note: Verbatim from Schoolcraft 1856, pp. 262-264; not verbatim (OCR modernized).

passages.text: Most of what is known on this subject is derived from Iagoo, who related that going out one day with his dogs to hunt, he passed through a wide range of thicket, where he lost his dogs. He became much alarmed, for they were faithful animals... At length he came to a spot where he found them asleep, having incautiously run near the residence of Weeng. After great exertions he aroused them, but not without having felt the power of somnolency himself. As he cast his eyes up from the place where the dogs were lying, he saw the Spirit of Sleep sitting upon the branch of a tree. He was in the shape of a giant insect, or monetos, with many wings from his back, which made a low deep murmuring sound, like distant falling water. But Iagoo himself, being a very great liar and braggart, but little credit was given to his narration.
passages.note: Verbatim from Schoolcraft 1856, p. 263; not verbatim (OCR modernized).

title.en: Addik Kum Maig: The Origin of the White Fish

region.en: Rapids of Pauwateeg (Sault Ste. Marie), upper Great Lakes
region.zh: 保瓦提格急流（蘇聖瑪麗），上大湖區

source.work: H. R. Schoolcraft, The Myth of Hiawatha, and Other Oral Legends (1856), 'Addik Kum Maig'

summary.en: A hunter's wife carries on a secret affair with a mysterious visitor who never walks the path nor carries food; warned by their sons, the father kills her with a war-club and buries her under the ashes of his fire. Her spirit and then her rolling skull haunt the sons down the shores of Lake Superior to the falls of Pauwateeg, where an aged crane ferries the persecuted brothers across - warning them not to touch the sore back of his head. The skull begs the same ferry, cannot resist touching the wound, and is thrown into the rapids: 'There... you shall now be changed into something for the benefit of your people, and it shall be called Addik Kum Maig.' As the skull floated from rock to rock the brains were strewed in the water, in a form resembling roes, which assumed the shape of a new species of fish possessing a whiteness of color and peculiar flavor.
summary.zh: 獵人之妻與一位不走路徑、不攜食物的神秘訪客私通；兒子們告知父親，他一棒擊斃妻子，葬於灶灰之下。她的魂魄與滾動的頭骨一路作祟，追著兒子們沿蘇必利爾湖岸逃至保瓦提格瀑布。一隻年邁的鶴渡二人過灘——囑咐切莫碰牠頭後的傷處。頭骨也求渡，卻忍不住碰了傷處，被擲入急流：「你生前毫無用處，如今化為造福你族之物，名為阿迪克庫梅格。」頭骨逐岩漂滾，腦髓散落水中，狀如魚卵，遂化作一種色白味美的新魚——白魚。

sensitivity.note: Schoolcraft 1856; public domain. Domestic violence is narrated as the crime's cause in story register.

passages.text: They noticed that a young man visited the lodge during their father's absence, and these visits were frequently repeated. At length the elder of the two said to his mother: 'My mother, who is this tall young man that comes here so often during our father's absence?' 'Bad boy,' said the mother, pettishly, 'mind your bow and arrows... Say not a word to him on the subject.' But as they grew older, and still saw the visits of this mysterious stranger, they resolved to speak again to their mother, and told her that they meant to inform their father of all they had observed, for they frequently saw this young man passing through the woods, and he did not walk in the path, nor did he carry anything to eat. At this the mother flew into a rage: 'I will kill you,' said she, 'if you speak of it.' They resolved at last to disclose the whole matter to their father. The result was such as might have been anticipated: the father, being satisfied of the infidelity of his wife, watched a suitable occasion, and with a single blow of his war-club dispatched her. He then buried her under the ashes of his fire, took down the lodge, and removed with his two sons to a distant position.
passages.note: Condensed from Schoolcraft 1856, pp. 265-266; not verbatim.

passages.text: But the spirit of the woman haunted the children, who were now grown up to the estate of young men. She appeared to them as they returned from hunting in the evening. They were also terrified in their dreams, which they attributed to her. Life became a scene of perpetual terrors. They resolved, together with their father, to leave the country, and commenced a journey toward the south. After travelling many days along the shores of Lake Superior, they passed around a high promontory of rock where a large river issued out of the lake, and soon after came to a place called Pauwateeg. They had no sooner come in sight of these falls than they beheld the skull of the woman rolling along the beach. They were in the utmost fear, and knew not how to elude her.
passages.note: Condensed from Schoolcraft 1856, pp. 266-267; not verbatim.

passages.text: At this moment one of them looked out, and saw a stately crane sitting on a rock in the middle of the rapids. They called out to the bird, 'See, grandfather, we are persecuted by a spirit. Come and take us across the falls, so that we may escape her.' This crane was a bird of extraordinary size and great age... 'Be careful,' said the crane, 'that you do not touch the back part of my head. It is sore, and should you press against it, I shall not be able to avoid throwing you both into the rapids.' They were, however, attentive on this point, and were safely landed on the south shore of the river. The crane then resumed his former position in the rapids. But the skull now cried out, 'Come, my grandfather, and carry me over, for I have lost my children, and am sorely distressed.' The aged bird flew to her assistance, and carefully repeated the injunction...
passages.note: Condensed from Schoolcraft 1856, pp. 267-268; not verbatim.

passages.text: She promised to obey, but soon felt a curiosity to know where the head of her carrier had been hurt... before they were half way over the rapids, she could not resist the inclination she felt to touch the affected part. Instantly the crane threw her into the rapids. 'There,' said he, 'you have been of no use during your life, you shall now be changed into something for the benefit of your people, and it shall be called Addik Kum Maig.' As the skull floated from rock to rock, the brains were strewed in the water, in a form resembling roes, which soon assumed the shape of a new species of fish, possessing a whiteness of color, and peculiar flavor, which have caused it, ever since, to be in great repute with the Indians.
passages.note: Condensed from Schoolcraft 1856, pp. 267-268; not verbatim.

title.en: The Enchanted Moccasins: Onwe Bahmondoong and the Sisters of the Tree Lodge
title.zh: 魔法鹿皮鞋：負球者與樹屋姊妹

region.en: Village of hunters with the smooth barkless tree, Odjibwa country
region.zh: 奧吉布瓦之地有光滑無皮大樹的獵村

source.work: H. R. Schoolcraft, The Myth of Hiawatha, and Other Oral Legends (1856), 'The Enchanted Moccasins'

summary.en: Onwe Bahmondoong, He That Carries a Ball on His Back, seeks the village from which no person has ever returned. An old woman warns him of the tree lodge hung with the chief's two daughters - Azhabee, She Who Sits Behind, who makes the tree descend, and Negahnahbee, She Who Sits Before, who makes it shoot to the arch of heaven - and gives him the medicine-dance bones by whose magic he can penetrate any substance. Speaking only to the left-hand sister, he brings the tree down, clubs the death-dealing sisters, and flees the avenging brother Mudjikewis: into a moose skeleton whose enchanted moccasins walk 'to the end of the earth' to mislead the pursuit, then into the disguise of a feeble old man in a garden lodge, whose daughters feed the starving pursuer - breaking his fast, and so destroying his power - until Onwe Bahmondoong resumes his youthful form and ends him with one blow of the magic ball.
summary.zh: 「負球者」翁威巴蒙東前往那座從無人歸返的村子。老嫗警告他樹上吊著酋長兩個女兒的小屋——左手的「居後者」阿扎比能令樹降，右手的「居前者」內甘內比則令樹直升天穹——並授予醫舞之骨，憑其魔法可穿透萬物。他只與左手那位說話，使樹垂下，擊斃害人的姊妹，逃離復仇的兄長穆吉維斯：先化為駝鹿骸骨，讓魔法鹿皮鞋「走到大地盡頭」以誤導追蹤；再化身花園木屋中的衰邁老人，兩個女兒餵食瀕餓的追者——追者破齋，法力盡失——負球者恢復少年之形，一擊畢命。

passages.text: There once lived a little boy, all alone with his sister, in a very wild uninhabitable country... the opinion was formed that he had supernatural powers, and he was called Onwe Bahmondoong, or he that carries a ball on his back. As he grew up he was impatient to know whether there were other beings near them... Being now well grown, he determined to seek his fortune, and asked her to make him several pairs of moccasins to last him on the journey. He travelled on, not knowing exactly where he went. At last he came to a small wigwam, and, on looking into it, discovered a very old woman sitting alone by the fire. 'My poor grandchild, I suppose you are one of those who seek for the distant village, from which no person has ever yet returned... Be careful to provide yourself with the Ozhebahguhnun - the bones they use in the medicine dance - without which you cannot succeed.'
passages.note: Condensed from Schoolcraft 1856, pp. 293-294; not verbatim.

passages.text: Before the door of the chief's lodge you will see a great tree, which is smooth and destitute of bark; on this tree, about the height of a man from the ground, a small lodge is suspended, in which the two daughters dwell. It is here so many have been destroyed. As often as he attempted to reach it, the tree began to tremble and soon shot up so that the lodge could hardly be perceived. He changed himself into a small squirrel and mounted the tree, thrusting one of the bones into the trunk as often as he became fatigued; but whenever he came near the lodge the tree would shoot up as before, until it had reached the arch of heaven and could go no higher. He entered the lodge and beheld the two sisters sitting opposite each other: the one on his left hand called herself Azhabee (one who sits behind), and the one on the right Negahnahbee (one who sits before). Whenever he addressed the one on his left hand, the tree would tremble and settle down to its former position; but when he addressed the one on his right hand, it would again shoot upward. Discovering this, he continued addressing the left-hand sister until the tree had resumed its former position; then seizing his war-club, 'You, who have caused the death of so many of my brothers, I will now put an end to' - and he laid them dead at his feet.
passages.note: Condensed from Schoolcraft 1856, pp. 294-296; not verbatim.

passages.text: Learning that the sisters had a brother living with their father who would pursue him for the deed, he set off at random. Mudjikewis replied, 'The person who has done this must be the Boy that carries the Ball on his Back. I will pursue him... Above all, avoid tasting food till you succeed; for if you break your fast before you see his blood, your power will be destroyed.' The pursued climbed up into one of the tallest trees and shot forth his magic arrows; finding that his pursuer was not turned back, he transformed himself into the skeleton of a moose that had been killed, whose flesh had come off from his bones. He then remembered the moccasins which his sister had given him, which were enchanted. Taking a pair of them, he placed them near the skeleton: 'Go,' said he to them, 'to the end of the earth.' The moccasins then left him and their tracks remained; Mudjikewis followed the track he had long been pursuing till he came to the end of the earth, where he found only a pair of moccasins.
passages.note: Condensed from Schoolcraft 1856, pp. 296-297; not verbatim.

passages.text: The other, finding he was closely pursued, now changed himself into a very old man, with two daughters, who lived in a large lodge in the centre of a beautiful garden, filled with everything that could delight the eye or was pleasant to the taste; he made himself appear so very old as to be unable to leave his lodge, and had his daughters to bring him food and wait on him. His pursuer continued on till he was nearly starved and ready to sink: 'Oh! I will forget the blood of my sisters, for I am starving'; but again he thought of the blood of his sisters, and again he resolved to pursue. At the beautiful garden the daughters invited him in, and boiled corn and prepared other savory food. Mudjikewis had no suspicion of the deception... he partook heartily of the meal, and in so doing was overcome: all at once he seemed to forget the blood of his sisters, and even the village of his nativity; he ate so heartily as to produce drowsiness, and soon fell into a profound sleep. Onwe Bahmondoong watched his opportunity, and as soon as he found his slumbers sound, resumed his youthful form; then he drew the magic ball from his back, which turned out to be a heavy war-club, with one blow of which he put an end to his pursuer, and thus vindicated his title as the Wearer of the Ball.
passages.note: Condensed from Schoolcraft 1856, pp. 297-298; not verbatim.

title.en: Leelinau: The Bride of the Fairy of Green Pines
title.zh: 莉莉娜：綠松仙子的新娘

region.en: Great sand dunes of Naigow Wudjoo (La Grandes Sables) and the manito wac, Spirit wood, Lake Superior
region.zh: 蘇必利爾湖畔奈戈伍吉大沙丘與「靈林」

texts.period: A Chippewa tale collected by Schoolcraft (1856)

source.work: H. R. Schoolcraft, The Myth of Hiawatha, and Other Oral Legends (1856), 'Leelinau'

summary.en: At the great sand dunes of Naigow Wudjoo the Pukwudjininees, fairies of Lake Superior, are seen in moonlight, skipping over the hills and leaving footprints no bigger than a child's; they delight in mischief - stealing a fisherman's paddle, plucking the hunter's feathers, pilfering his game. From their sacred grove, the manito wac, they entice away a chief's pensive, sylph-like daughter, Leelinau, who pines for a land of no weeping, no cares, and no deaths, and deems the light little men emissaries from the Happy Land. Her mother matches her with a neighboring forester; dressed in her finest, with flowers in her hair, she asks one request - a farewell visit to the sacred grove before the nuptial bower. The bridegroom waits in vain: a fisherman conceives he saw her go off with one of the tall fairies known as the fairy of Green Pines, with green plumes nodding o'er his brows - and it is supposed she is still roving with him over the elysian fields.
summary.zh: 蘇必利爾湖畔奈戈伍吉大沙丘，是小人族「帕克伍吉尼內斯」的名居；月明之夜，漁人常見他們在丘間跳躍，沙上留下孩童大小的足印。他們頑皮搗蛋——偷漿、拔羽、竊獵物。自他們的聖林「靈林」，他們誘走酋長那位沉思如精靈的女兒莉莉娜——她渴望一個無淚、無憂、無死亡之地，把這些輕快的小人視作福地的使者。母親為她許配鄰近的獵人；婚禮之夜，她一身盛裝、髮插花朵，只求在入洞房前到仙林作別。新郎苦候無果：一位漁人自稱見她隨一位高大仙者而去——那人便是眉際綠羽點點的「綠松仙子」——相傳她至今仍在極樂原野與他雙雙漫遊。

passages.text: The Pukwudjininees, or fairies of Lake Superior, had one of their most noted places of residence at the great sand dunes of Naigow Wudjoo, called by the French La Grandes Sables. Here they were frequently seen in bright moonlight evenings, and the fishermen while sitting in their canoes on the lake often saw them playing their pranks, and skipping over the hills. There was a grove of pines in that vicinity called the manito wac, or Spirit wood, into which they might be seen to flee, on the approach of evening, and there is a romantic little lake on those elevated sand-hills, on the shores of which their tracks could be plainly seen in the sand. These tracks were not bigger than little children's footprints, and the spirits were often seen in the act of vanishing behind the little pine-trees. They love to dance in the most lonesome places, and were always full of glee and merriment.
passages.note: Verbatim from Schoolcraft 1856, p. 299; not verbatim (OCR modernized).

passages.text: These little men, the pukwudjininees, are not deeply malicious, but rather delighted in mischief and freaks, and would sometimes steal away a fisherman's paddle, or come at night and pluck the hunter's feathers out of his cap in the lodge, or pilfer away some of his game, or fish. On one occasion they went so far as to entice away into their sacred grove, and carry off a chief's daughter - a small but beautiful girl, who had been always inclined to be pensive, and took her seat often in these lonesome haunts. From her baby name of Neenizu, my dear life, she was called Leelinau, but she never attained to much size, remaining very slender, but of the most pleasing and sylph-like features, with very bright black eyes, and little feet.
passages.note: Verbatim from Schoolcraft 1856, pp. 299-300; not verbatim (OCR modernized).

passages.text: She had imbibed ideas of a spiritual life and existence, which she fancied could only be enjoyed in the Indian elysium, and instructed as she was by the old story-tellers, she could not do otherwise than deem the light and sprightly little men who made the fairy footprints as emissaries from the Happy Land. For this happy land she sighed and pined. Blood, and the taking of life, she said, the Great Spirit did not approve... And she longed to go to a region where there was no weeping, no cares, and no deaths... She announced her willingness to accede to the matrimonial proposals, and the day was fixed. She dressed herself in the finest manner possible, putting flowers in her hair, and carrying a bunch of wild flowers, mixed with tassels of the pine-tree in her hand.
passages.note: Verbatim from Schoolcraft 1856, pp. 300-301; not verbatim (OCR modernized).

passages.text: One only request she made, which was to make a farewell visit to the sacred grove of the fairies, before she visited the nuptial bower. This was granted, on the evening of the proposed ceremony, while the bridegroom and his friends gathered in her father's lodge, and impatiently waited her return. But they waited in vain. Night came, but Leelinau was never more seen, except by a fisherman on the lake shore, who conceived that he had seen her go off with one of the tall fairies known as the fairy of Green Pines, with green plumes nodding o'er his brows; and it is supposed that she is still roving with him over the elysian fields.
passages.note: Verbatim from Schoolcraft 1856, pp. 300-301; not verbatim (OCR modernized).
